  "claims": [
    {
      "id": "f1",
      "concept_id": "c1",
      "text": "A checkpoint transfers transactions appended to the WAL back into the original database.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "Moving the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a \" checkpoint \".",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f2",
      "concept_id": "c3",
      "text": "SQLite's default automatic checkpoint threshold is 1000 pages.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "By default, SQLite does a checkpoint automatically when the WAL file reaches a threshold size of 1000 pages.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f3",
      "concept_id": "c1",
      "text": "A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, but must stop before a WAL page beyond a current reader's end mark.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f4",
      "concept_id": "c1",
      "text": "A long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "Thus a long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f5",
      "concept_id": "c1",
      "text": "A checkpointer records its progress in the wal-index and resumes from that point on a later invocation.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "The checkpoint remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got and will resume transferring content from the WAL to the database from where it left off on the next invocation.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f6",
      "concept_id": "c1",
      "text": "A writer can rewind the WAL only after all WAL content has been transferred and synced and no readers use the WAL.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f7",
      "concept_id": "c5",
      "text": "SQLite must sync the WAL before transferring its content into the database, and sync the database before resetting the WAL.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f8",
      "concept_id": "c3",
      "text": "SQLite automatically checkpoints when a COMMIT makes the WAL at least 1000 pages or when the last database connection closes.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "By default, SQLite will automatically checkpoint whenever a COMMIT occurs that causes the WAL file to be 1000 pages or more in size, or when the last database connection on a database file closes.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f9",
      "concept_id": "c2",
      "text": "PASSIVE checkpoints do as much work as possible without interfering with other connections and may not finish when readers or writers are concurrent.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "The default checkpoint style is PASSIVE, which does as much work as it can without interfering with other database connections, and which might not run to completion if there are concurrent readers or writers.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f10",
      "concept_id": "c5",
      "text": "WAL reads slow as the WAL grows, so regular checkpoints help maintain read performance.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "Hence, to maintain good read performance it is important to keep the WAL file size down by running checkpoints at regular intervals.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f11",
      "concept_id": "c2",
      "text": "PASSIVE checkpoints do not wait for readers or writers, do not invoke the busy handler, and sync the database if all log frames were checkpointed.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed. The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode.",
      "pass": 1
    },
    {
      "id": "f12",
      "concept_id": "c2",
      "text": "FULL waits for no writer and for all readers to use the most recent snapshot, then checkpoints all log frames and syncs the database.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot. It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file.",
      "pass": 1
    },
    {
      "id": "f13",
      "concept_id": "c2",
      "text": "FULL blocks new writers while pending but allows new readers to continue.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.",
      "pass": 1
    },
    {
      "id": "f14",
      "concept_id": "c2",
      "text": "RESTART behaves like FULL, then waits until all readers use only the database file so the next writer can restart the log at its beginning.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.",
      "pass": 1
    },
    {
      "id": "f15",
      "concept_id": "c2",
      "text": "TRUNCATE behaves like RESTART and truncates the log to zero bytes before successful return.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.",
      "pass": 1
    },
    {
      "id": "f16",
      "concept_id": "c2",
      "text": "NOOP checkpoints zero frames and can be used to read log and checkpointed frame counts through output parameters.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.",
      "pass": 1
    },
    {
      "id": "f17",
      "concept_id": "c2",
      "text": "Every checkpoint call takes an exclusive checkpoint lock; contention with another checkpoint returns SQLITE_BUSY without invoking the busy handler.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.",
      "pass": 1
    },
    {
      "id": "f18",
      "concept_id": "c2",
      "text": "FULL, RESTART, and TRUNCATE also acquire the exclusive writer lock; if reader-waiting or writer-lock busy handling gives up, they proceed like PASSIVE and return SQLITE_BUSY.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE - checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further. SQLITE_BUSY is returned in this case.",
      "pass": 1
    },
    {
      "id": "f19",
      "concept_id": "c3",
      "text": "sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint triggers after a commit when the WAL has at least N frames; zero or negative N disables automatic checkpoints.",
      "source_id": "S3",
      "quote": "The sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) is a wrapper around sqlite3_wal_hook() that causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.",
      "pass": 1
    },
    {
      "id": "f20",
      "concept_id": "c3",
      "text": "Registering sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint replaces an existing WAL hook, while registering a WAL hook disables the configured automatic checkpoint.",
      "source_id": "S3",
      "quote": "The callback registered by this function replaces any existing callback registered using sqlite3_wal_hook() . Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.",
      "pass": 1
    },
    {
      "id": "f21",
      "concept_id": "c3",
      "text": "Each new connection defaults to automatic checkpointing at 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.",
      "source_id": "S3",
      "quote": "Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.",
      "pass": 1
    },
    {
      "id": "f22",
      "concept_id": "c4",
      "text": "If overlapping readers ensure at least one reader is always active, checkpoints cannot complete and the WAL can grow without bound.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.",
      "pass": 2
    },
    {
      "id": "f23",
      "concept_id": "c4",
      "text": "Scheduling checkpoints during reader gaps can avoid starvation caused by continuously active readers.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are \"reader gaps\": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.",
      "pass": 2
    },
    {
      "id": "f24",
      "concept_id": "c4",
      "text": "RESTART and TRUNCATE can be used for manual checkpoints that wait for completion before returning, but readers might block while they run.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "In applications with many concurrent readers, one might also consider running manual checkpoints with the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART or SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE option which will ensure that the checkpoint runs to completion before returning. The disadvantage of using SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE is that readers might block while the checkpoint is running.",
      "pass": 2
    },
    {
      "id": "f25",
      "concept_id": "c4",
      "text": "A large write transaction prevents WAL reset until the transaction completes, so it can temporarily produce a large WAL.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "A checkpoint can only complete when no other transactions are running, which means the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction. So a large change to a large database might result in a large WAL file.",
      "pass": 2
    },
    {
      "id": "f26",
      "concept_id": "c4",
      "text": "Since SQLite 3.11.0, one transaction's WAL size should be proportional to the transaction because changed pages are written once; older versions could write a page repeatedly when cache capacity was exceeded.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "As of SQLite version 3.11.0 (2016-02-15), the WAL file for a single transaction should be proportional in size to the transaction itself. Pages that are changed by the transaction should only be written into the WAL file once.",
      "pass": 2
    },
    {
      "id": "f27",
      "concept_id": "c5",
      "text": "Checkpoint frequency trades read performance against write performance: frequent checkpoints keep the WAL small, while infrequent checkpoints amortize checkpoint cost across more writes.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "To maximize the read performance, one wants to keep the WAL as small as possible and hence run checkpoints frequently, perhaps as often as every COMMIT. To maximize write performance, one wants to amortize the cost of each checkpoint over as many writes as possible",
      "pass": 2
    },
    {
      "id": "f28",
      "concept_id": "c5",
      "text": "Checkpoints are slower than write transactions because they require syncs and typically intersperse database page writes with seeks.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "Checkpoint also requires more seeking. The checkpointer makes an effort to do as many sequential page writes to the database as it can (the pages are transferred from WAL to database in ascending order) but even then there will typically be many seek operations interspersed among the page writes.",
      "pass": 2
    },
    {
      "id": "f29",
      "concept_id": "c3",
      "text": "Automatic checkpoints are PASSIVE and run by the same thread as the COMMIT that crosses the default threshold, making most commits fast and occasional triggering commits slower.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "By default, the checkpoint will be run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit. This has the effect of causing most COMMIT operations to be very fast but an occasional COMMIT (those that trigger a checkpoint) to be much slower.",
      "pass": 2
    },
    {
      "id": "f30",
      "concept_id": "c5",
      "text": "With synchronous=NORMAL, moving checkpoints to a separate thread or process keeps the main database thread from blocking on a sync, but transactions may roll back after power loss or hard reset.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "If an application therefore runs checkpoint in a separate thread or process, the main thread or process that is doing database queries and updates will never block on a sync operation.",
      "pass": 2
    }
  ],
